title: His approach to writing for strings
summary: Think like a musician; consult the player.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: What's your philosophy for writing on strings?
No different than writing for anything else, except--no, no except. Strings have a quality that have to be strings (inaudible).

Yeah. (inaudible) The violin really depends on the player, as does everything else. The violin itself does nothing, it's a means to produce a sound and you have physical limitations to produce that sound, and you have to think of that, but not too much. (Inaudible). You shouldn't do certain things

that are obviously--that can be done the same thing in a simpler fashion--you can always try to do that, but I don't think that you need to be an accomplished violinist to do these things. You need to have the ability to think musically, and I think the violinist will respect what you've done (inaudible).

That's why almost all composers that I know, have always consulted whoever they're writing the piece for before they eventually let the publishing be done. Sometimes they'll redraft it three or four times because of things like that.

You must think that there is a guy behind every horn, a human being who has to eat, he has to take air, he has to move his fingers, purse his lips however. Different instruments speak in a different fashion; you have to know that.
